newsitem.title: USA: Florida freeze victims look to Washington for help.
newsitem.headline: Florida freeze victims look to Washington for help.

text.p: Florida agriculture officials estimate cold weather in mid-January may have caused up to $300 million in damage to the state's fresh fruit, vegetable and citrus crop.

As growers and state officials await word from Washington about federal disaster relief, attention is turning toward the plight of farm workers and whether federal cuts to the National Weather Service last year prompted greater losses from killer frost that cut a swathe through much of south Florida.

State agriculture officials estimate damage to the Florida fruit and vegetable crop will top $200 million. A further $100 million has been projected for Florida citrus, sugar cane and livestock industries, said Bob Blankenship, spokesman for the Florida Department of Agriculture.

In Dade County, which sustained an estimated $97 million in damages, farm officials are anxiously awaiting word from Washington over federal disaster relief. With 66 percent of the fruit and vegetable crops lost in Dade County, nearly 30,000 farm workers who would normally be working the height of the season are now having trouble finding work at all.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture is looking at its assistance options, including waiving rents on government-owner housing, food stamps or possible cash payments to workers, said Tom Kirby, government affairs director for the Dade County Farm Bureau.
Any federal disaster aid would have to be approved by U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman.
"Even the federal loan programme can't begin until the disaster declaration is signed," Kirby said. "No relief can begin, period, until it is."
Statewide damage estimates for individual crops are still being compiled and it may be weeks before a detailed assessment is available, state officials say.

In Dade County, nearly 100 percent of the green bean crop, 85 percent of squash and nearly all sweet potatoes were lost to the freeze. Growers are pointing fingers at Congress, which last year cut off funding for the National Weather Service's agriculture reporting service, a $3 million programme that until last spring provided growers across the country with weather forecasts tailored toward their specific needs.

Many growers said the freezing temperatures took them completely by surprise. They would have benefited from the agriculture reporting service's more detailed weather forecast, said Ray Gilmer, spokesman for the Florida Fruit and Vegetable Association, an Orlando-based growers group.
"Water is one of the key tools in fighting freezing conditions," Gilmer said. "But it takes farmers time to set up their systems. In this case they didn't have enough time."
Crop damage not only affected farmers, but took a toll on trucking lines and other related industries that support growers during the height of the season.
"When you look at the lost revenue to government alone, maybe Congress was penny-wise and pound foolish," Kirby said.
